usage: 사업하다 also works as one verb; 사업을 하다 splits it with the object marker
시작하다 = to begin; common with launching a venture
잘되다 (one word) = to go well; 사업이 안되다 = to do badly
계획 = plan; 사업 모델, 사업 분야 also use 사업 as a modifier
examples: 저는 작은 온라인 사업을 시작하려고 해요.
I'm planning to start a small online business.
V-(으)려고 하다 = intend to; 작은 modifies 사업
요즘 경기가 안 좋아서 사업이 잘 안돼요.
Business isn't going well these days because the economy is bad.
안돼요 = isn't going well; -아서/어서 gives the reason
그분은 사업으로 크게 성공한 사람이에요.
He's someone who succeeded big in business.
사업으로 = through/in business; 성공하다 = to succeed
nuance: 사업 is business as an undertaking or venture — running a company, a commercial project, or being self-employed. It is broader and more concrete than 산업 (industry as a sector) and refers to what an individual or company actively does. A government or public project is also called 사업 (예: 복지 사업, welfare project).
mistakes: Don't confuse 사업 (a business/venture you run) with 산업 (an industry sector like 자동차 산업).
사업하다 is one verb, but when you add an object marker you must split it: 사업을 하다, not 사업하다를.

usage: 산업 follows the field as a modifier: 반도체 산업, 관광 산업
발전하다 = to develop/advance; 산업이 성장하다 also common
구조 = structure; describes how an economy's sectors are organized
첨단 = cutting-edge; contrasts with 전통 산업 (traditional industry)
examples: 한국은 반도체 산업이 매우 발달해 있어요.
Korea's semiconductor industry is very advanced.
발달해 있다 = is (in a state of being) developed; V-아/어 있다 for resulting state
요즘은 인공지능 관련 산업이 빠르게 성장하고 있어요.
These days AI-related industries are growing fast.
관련 = related; -고 있다 for ongoing change
이 도시는 관광 산업으로 유명해요.
This city is famous for its tourism industry.
(으)로 유명하다 = famous for
nuance: 산업 refers to an industry as a whole sector of the economy (manufacturing, tourism, IT), not a single company. Use it for macro-level talk about the economy. 사업 is what a specific business does; 산업 is the field that many businesses belong to. You will see it constantly in news and formal writing.
mistakes: 산업 is a sector, so don't say 산업을 시작하다 to mean 'start a business' — use 사업을 시작하다.
Avoid the romanization-driven mix-up: 산업 = industry, 사업 = business; the 'ㄴ' vs 'ㅏ' difference matters.

usage: 경력이 없다 = to have no experience; counts as professional track record
number + 년 after 경력 states length of career
-직 = position; contrasts with 신입 (new graduate hire)
examples: 이 일은 관련 경력이 3년 이상 필요해요.
This job requires at least 3 years of relevant experience.
이상 = or more; 필요하다 = to be needed
저는 마케팅 분야에서 경력을 쌓고 싶어요.
I want to build my career in the marketing field.
분야에서 = in the field of; -고 싶다 = want to
경력이 많을수록 연봉도 높아져요.
The more experience you have, the higher the salary gets.
-(으)ㄹ수록 = the more...the more; 높아지다 = to become higher
nuance: 경력 means accumulated professional experience or work history — what goes on a résumé. It differs from 경험 (경험, any experience, including everyday or one-time experiences). For a job application, you list your 경력; a fun trip is a 경험, not 경력. 경력직 (experienced hire) is a key word in Korean hiring.
mistakes: Don't swap 경력 with 경험: 경력 = professional track record, 경험 = experience in general (already in beginner vocab).
경력 is counted in years with 년 (경력 3년), not with 번 or 개.

usage: 직원을 채용하다 = to hire an employee
공고 = public notice; where openings are announced
신입 = entry-level; 경력 채용 = experienced-hire recruitment
passive sense; 채용 과정 = hiring process
examples: 그 회사는 올해 신입 사원을 많이 채용할 거예요.
That company will hire a lot of new employees this year.
V-(으)ㄹ 거예요 = will; 사원 = staff member
채용 공고를 보고 지원서를 냈어요.
I saw the job posting and submitted an application.
-고 = and then; 지원서를 내다 = to submit an application
요즘은 경력직 채용이 신입 채용보다 더 많아요.
These days experienced-hire recruitment is more common than new-graduate recruitment.
N보다 더 = more than
nuance: 채용 is the formal word for recruitment/hiring used by companies — you see it in 채용 공고 (job postings) and 채용 과정 (hiring process). It is more institutional than the casual 뽑다 (to pick/select, already known). A company 채용한다; the applicant 지원한다 (applies). 입사하다 (already in vocab) is the applicant joining after being hired.
mistakes: 채용하다 is what the company does (hires); the applicant 지원하다 (applies) — don't reverse them.
Don't write 채용 as 체용; the first syllable is 채 (ㅐ).

usage: 수입이 적다 = to have a low income
줄다 = to decrease; 수입이 늘다 = income increases
한 달 = one month; states the period of income
지출 (already in vocab) = spending; common budgeting pair
examples: 프리랜서는 매달 수입이 일정하지 않아요.
A freelancer's income isn't steady every month.
일정하다 = to be fixed/steady; -지 않다 = negative
부수입을 올리려고 주말에 아르바이트를 해요.
I work a part-time job on weekends to earn extra income.
부수입 = side income; 올리다 = to raise/earn
수입보다 지출이 많으면 저축하기 어려워요.
If spending exceeds income, it's hard to save.
N보다 = than; -기 어렵다 = hard to do
nuance: 수입 most often means income or revenue (money coming in), contrasted with 지출 (spending). Note it is a homograph: 수입(輸入) also means imports (the opposite of 수출, exports), distinguished only by context. For personal money, think 수입 = earnings. 소득 (already in vocab) is a near-synonym for income, often used in formal/statistical contexts (예: 소득세, income tax).
mistakes: 수입 means both 'income' and 'imports' — context decides; don't assume one meaning without checking the sentence.
Don't confuse 수입 (income/imports) with 수출 (exports); 입 = enter, 출 = exit.

usage: 보다 here = to incur; the standard collocation
입다 = to suffer (formal); 손해를 끼치다 = to cause loss to someone
크다/적다 describe the size of the loss
examples: 지금 팔면 손해를 볼 것 같아서 좀 더 기다리려고요.
I think I'll lose money if I sell now, so I'm going to wait a bit longer.
V-(으)ㄹ 것 같다 = seems like; -(으)려고요 = I intend to
회사가 이번 투자로 큰 손해를 입었어요.
The company suffered a big loss from this investment.
투자로 = from/through the investment; 입다 = to sustain
환불해 주지 않으면 소비자가 손해를 봐요.
If they don't refund it, the consumer takes the loss.
-아/어 주다 = do for someone; 소비자 = consumer
nuance: 손해 is a loss or damage, almost always financial or in terms of disadvantage — the opposite of 이익/이득 (profit/gain). The set phrase 손해를 보다 ('to take a loss') is essential and very frequent. Use 손해 for money lost or a deal where you come out worse; for physical breakage use 고장 or 피해 instead.
mistakes: Use 손해를 보다 (with 보다) for 'to suffer a loss' — learners often wrongly say 손해를 하다.
손해 is about loss/disadvantage; don't use it for physical breakage (use 고장/피해).

usage: 오르다/떨어지다 for value going up/down (e.g., property, stocks)
예: 볼 가치가 있다 = worth seeing
examples: 이 경험은 돈으로 살 수 없는 가치가 있어요.
This experience has a value that money can't buy.
V-(으)ㄹ 수 없다 = cannot; 가치가 있다 = has value
그 그림은 시간이 지날수록 가치가 올라갔어요.
That painting rose in value as time passed.
-(으)ㄹ수록 = the more...; 올라가다 = to go up
저는 일을 고를 때 연봉보다 가치를 더 중요하게 생각해요.
When I choose a job, I value meaning more than salary.
고를 때 = when choosing; 중요하게 생각하다 = to consider important
nuance: 가치 means value or worth — both economic value (가치가 오르다, rises in value) and abstract worth (인생의 가치, the value of life). The pattern V-(으)ㄹ 가치가 있다 ('worth doing') is extremely useful. 가치관 (one's values/worldview) is a high-frequency derived word. Distinguish from 가격 (가격, price tag) and 값 (value/cost), which are concrete amounts.
mistakes: Don't confuse 가치 (worth/value, abstract or economic) with 가격 (the listed price, already in vocab).
For 'worth doing', use V-(으)ㄹ 가치가 있다, not 가치가 하다.

usage: 높이다 = to raise; 품질을 관리하다 = to manage quality
examples: 가격은 조금 비싸지만 품질이 정말 좋아요.
It's a bit pricey, but the quality is really good.
-지만 = but; 정말 = really
요즘 소비자들은 가격보다 품질을 더 따져요.
These days consumers scrutinize quality more than price.
따지다 (already in vocab) = to scrutinize; N보다 더 = more than
품질을 높이려면 생산 과정을 개선해야 해요.
To improve quality, you need to improve the production process.
-(으)려면 = if you want to; -아/어야 하다 = must
nuance: 품질 refers specifically to the quality of goods or products — how well-made something is. It is the standard word in 품질 관리 (quality control) and product reviews. Don't use 품질 for the quality of an abstract thing like life or sleep; for those Koreans say 삶의 질 or 수면의 질 (using 질, quality). 품(品) signals 'goods', so 품질 = goods-quality.
mistakes: Use 품질 for product quality, but 삶의 질 (not 삶의 품질) for 'quality of life'.
품질이 좋다/나쁘다 describes quality; 품질을 잘하다 is wrong (it's a noun state, not an action).

usage: 대량 = large quantity; 소량 생산 = small-batch production
라인, 과정 follow 생산 as compounds
examples: 이 공장에서는 하루에 자동차를 천 대 생산해요.
This factory produces a thousand cars a day.
에서는 = at (location, topic); 대 = counter for vehicles
원자재 가격이 올라서 생산 비용이 늘었어요.
Production costs rose because raw material prices went up.
원자재 = raw materials; 비용 (already in vocab) = cost
수요가 많아지면 생산을 더 늘려야 해요.
When demand grows, you have to increase production.
수요 = demand; 늘리다 = to increase (transitive)
nuance: 생산 means production or manufacturing — making goods. It pairs naturally with 소비 (consumption) as the supply side of the economy (생산과 소비). Use 대량 생산 for mass production. The agent who produces is a 생산자 (producer), opposite of 소비자 (consumer). Keep 생산 (making things) distinct from 산업 (the industry sector) and 사업 (a business venture).
mistakes: 생산 is making/output; don't use it to mean 'industry' (산업) or 'business' (사업).
To increase production use 생산을 늘리다 (transitive 늘리다), not 생산을 늘다 (intransitive).

usage: 늘다/줄다 for spending rising or falling
과- = excessive; 합리적 소비 = sensible consumption
examples: 경기가 나빠지면 사람들은 소비를 줄여요.
When the economy worsens, people cut back on spending.
나빠지다 = to get worse; 줄이다 = to reduce
요즘 젊은 소비자들은 환경을 많이 생각해요.
These days young consumers think a lot about the environment.
소비자 = consumer; 생각하다 = to think about
과소비를 줄이려고 가계부를 쓰기 시작했어요.
I started keeping a budget book to cut down on overspending.
-(으)려고 = in order to; 가계부 (already in vocab) = budget book
nuance: 소비 means consumption or spending — using up money, goods, or resources. It is the demand-side counterpart to 생산 (production), and 소비자 (consumer) is one of the most useful derived words. Distinguish from 지출 (지출, an outlay/expenditure entry) and 낭비하다 (to waste, already in vocab): 소비 can be neutral or even necessary, while 낭비 is always negative.
mistakes: 소비 (consumption, can be neutral) is not the same as 낭비 (waste, always negative).
To reduce spending use 소비를 줄이다 (transitive 줄이다), not 소비를 줄다.

usage: 짜다 = to put together/plan; the idiomatic verb for budgets
부족하다 = to be short; 예산이 남다 = budget is left over
세우다 = to set up; 예산을 초과하다 = to exceed the budget
안에서 = inside; 예산을 넘다 = to go over budget
examples: 이번 여행은 예산이 부족해서 호텔 대신 게스트하우스에 묵었어요.
I was short on budget for this trip, so I stayed at a guesthouse instead of a hotel.
대신 = instead of; 묵다 = to stay (lodge)
회사에서 내년 마케팅 예산을 줄이기로 했어요.
The company decided to cut next year's marketing budget.
-기로 하다 = to decide to; 줄이다 = to reduce
예산을 미리 짜 두면 돈을 더 잘 관리할 수 있어요.
If you plan a budget in advance, you can manage money better.
-아/어 두다 = do in advance; V-(으)ㄹ 수 있다 = can
nuance: 예산 is a budget — a planned amount of money for a project, household, or organization. The collocation 예산을 짜다 ('to put a budget together') is the most natural verb; 예산을 세우다 also works. Distinguish from 가계부 (the actual record of what was spent) and 비용 (the cost incurred). 예산 is the plan; 지출 is what actually goes out.
mistakes: Use 예산을 짜다 or 예산을 세우다 for 'make a budget'; 예산을 만들다 sounds unnatural.
예산 is the planned amount (a plan), not the money already spent (지출/비용).

usage: 부족하다 = to lack; common startup problem
투자하다 = to invest; 자본을 모으다 = to raise capital
-금 = money/funds; the founding capital of a company
examples: 사업을 시작하려면 어느 정도 자본이 필요해요.
To start a business, you need a certain amount of capital.
-(으)려면 = if you want to; 어느 정도 = a certain degree
그들은 적은 자본으로 회사를 크게 키웠어요.
They grew the company big with little capital.
적은 = small/little; 키우다 = to grow (something)
외국 자본이 한국 시장에 많이 들어왔어요.
A lot of foreign capital has entered the Korean market.
들어오다 = to come in; 시장 (already in vocab) = market
nuance: 자본 is capital in the economic sense — the money and assets used to run or start a business. It is more abstract and formal than 돈 (money) or 자금 (funds for a specific purpose). 자본금 (paid-in capital) and 자본주의 (capitalism) are key derived terms. You need 자본 to start a 사업 (business); without enough, 자본이 부족하다.
mistakes: 자본 is business capital/assets, not everyday cash — for general money use 돈, for earmarked funds use 자금.
Don't drop the final consonant: it's 자본 (with ㄴ), not 자보.
